inputs.need:
I am the infection prevention lead at a 620-bed teaching hospital. Last year we installed an electronic hand hygiene monitoring system on 16 adult medical and surgical wards: staff wear badges that log each alcohol rub or soap dispenser use and each entry into a patient zone. So far the system only collects data and nobody sees it. The vendor says that switching on real-time feedback (the badge vibrates if there is no hand hygiene within ten seconds of entering a patient zone) together with weekly ward dashboards raises compliance, and the hospital board wants to buy the feedback licence for every ward. I am not convinced. Our own observation rounds by trained observers show 62 percent compliance, but the observers are visible and staff know when they are there.

I want to run a cluster randomised trial across the 16 wards: eight wards switch on real-time feedback and dashboards and eight continue silent monitoring, for six months. The difficulty is the outcome. If we use the system's own compliance figure, feedback wards may learn to satisfy the badge without cleaning their hands, and the silent wards' figures would not be comparable. Direct observation is expensive and staff behave differently when watched. Infection rates such as MRSA acquisition or hospital-onset C. difficile are too rare on 16 wards to show a difference in six months.

I need help with the primary outcome, how to limit contamination (float nurses and junior doctors work across wards), the sample size given clustering, whether individual staff consent is needed when the badges already collect data under an agreement with the staff council, and how to present all this to the board, who want an answer by June 2027. The unions agreed to the monitoring only on condition that badge data are never used for individual performance management.
inputs.constraints: Six-month trial window from January to June 2027; 16 wards only; 400 hours of independent observer time; badge data may be used at ward level only, never for individual performance management.
localFacts: The infection prevention committee endorsed a ward-randomised comparison of badge feedback on 2026-09-15 (minute IPC-2026-22).
Joint staff council agreement JSC-2026-07 permits ward-level use of badge data for evaluation and forbids individual performance management.
About 20 percent of nursing shifts on the 16 wards are worked by float staff who move between wards.
Trained observers from the regional infection prevention network can provide 400 observer-hours between January and June 2027.

response.title: Real-time electronic hand hygiene feedback on 16 hospital wards
response.subtitle: Cluster randomised trial with an outcome measured independently of the feedback system
response.statement: The hospital board intends to buy a real-time feedback licence for badge-based hand hygiene monitoring on all 16 wards on the strength of vendor claims. Whether feedback improves actual hand hygiene, rather than the badge system's own compliance figure, is unknown locally, and the obvious outcomes are biased: the system's figure can be gamed on feedback wards, visible observers change behaviour, and infections are too rare to compare in six months. A ward-randomised comparison with an outcome measured independently of the feedback system would answer the board's question.
response.whoAffected: Patients on 16 adult medical and surgical wards, the nurses, doctors and float staff who wear the badges, the infection prevention team, and the board deciding on the licence.
response.whatHurts: Poor hand hygiene spreads resistant organisms and C. difficile between patients. Buying feedback that changes the badge figure but not hand hygiene would cost money and staff goodwill, and alerts that feel like surveillance could damage trust in the monitoring agreement.
response.currentPractice: Silent badge monitoring on 16 wards with no feedback to staff; periodic visible observation rounds reporting 62 percent compliance; infection rates reported monthly.
response.whyNow: A board decision on the licence is due by June 2027, the badge system is already installed on all 16 wards, and 400 hours of independent observer time are available from January.
response.constraints: Six months from January to June 2027; 16 wards; 400 observer-hours; badge data at ward level only under agreement JSC-2026-07; no individual performance management.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Patients on every ward are cared for by staff who clean their hands at the moments that prevent transmission, whether or not anyone is watching.
response.summary: Problem framed as a ward-randomised comparison of real-time feedback with an outcome independent of the badge system.

records.title: Real-time feedback from electronic hand hygiene monitoring on medical wards: a cluster randomised trial
records.authors: Okafor-Lindahl S, Brennan-Tshabalala M, Iwata-Moreau J
records.abstract: Methods: twelve medical wards with badge-based hand hygiene monitoring were randomised to real-time vibration feedback with weekly ward dashboards or to silent monitoring for six months. The primary outcome was compliance recorded by the electronic system at patient-zone entry. Results: electronic compliance rose from 48 to 71 percent on feedback wards and from 50 to 54 percent on control wards (difference in change 19 percentage points, 95 percent CI 11 to 27). Directly observed compliance, a secondary outcome measured on a random sample of shifts, was 64 against 57 percent. Healthcare-associated infections were too few for comparison. Conclusions: real-time feedback increased hand hygiene compliance.

records.title: Visible observers and dispenser activity on four wards: observed hand hygiene compared with concurrent covert counts
records.abstract: On four wards we compared hand hygiene events counted covertly by dispenser sensors during hours when a trained observer was visibly present with the same hours on days without an observer. Dispenser events per hour were about three times higher when an observer was present, and the increase was confined to the area within the observer's line of sight. Compliance recorded by the observer was 78 percent, whereas covert counts implied a much lower rate. The effect did not fade over eight weeks of observation. Observer-based compliance therefore measures behaviour under observation rather than usual behaviour, and comparisons between groups are fair only if observation is equally visible in both.

records.title: Badge and dispenser-based hand hygiene monitoring: a review of 31 evaluations of detection accuracy and feedback
records.authors: Harrow-Delacroix P, Nwosu-Ekberg L, Tanaka-Fitzgerald R
records.abstract: We included 31 studies of electronic or automated hand hygiene monitoring systems. Accuracy against direct observation varied widely: badge systems detected between 53 and 91 percent of observed hand hygiene opportunities, and most missed opportunities during continuous care within a patient zone. Fourteen studies reported compliance after feedback was introduced; twelve reported improvement, but only two were randomised and most used the monitoring system's own measure as the outcome. No study showed a reduction in infections with adequate power. We recommend an outcome measured independently of the feedback system in any comparative evaluation.

records.title: Badge-based hand hygiene monitoring and nurse acceptability on two surgical wards
records.abstract: We asked nurses on two surgical wards about badge-based monitoring six months after it was introduced, using group discussions with 22 nurses and a short questionnaire returned by 61 of 94 nursing staff. Most accepted ward-level feedback but objected strongly to managers seeing individual data. Several nurses described touching a dispenser near the door to stop the badge vibrating during busy periods, without cleaning their hands. Night staff said vibration alerts woke patients in shared bays. Nurses asked for the rules on data use to be written down and agreed with staff representatives before any expansion of the system.

records.title: Healthcare-associated infection rates after hand hygiene feedback dashboards: an interrupted time series in a regional hospital
records.abstract: We examined monthly counts of MRSA acquisition and hospital-onset C. difficile infection over 24 months before and 18 months after ward hand hygiene dashboards were introduced in a 480-bed hospital. Events averaged 3.1 per month across the hospital. There was no clear change in level or slope after the dashboards, and the confidence intervals were compatible with anything from a 30 percent reduction to a 20 percent increase. Hand rub consumption rose by 12 percent. The authors conclude that infection outcomes are too infrequent in a single hospital to evaluate hand hygiene interventions over short periods.

records.title: Intracluster correlation coefficients for hand hygiene compliance in ward-randomised studies
records.abstract: We estimated intracluster correlation coefficients from the individual observation data of six ward-randomised and cluster-level studies of hand hygiene. For compliance measured by direct observation, the intracluster correlation ranged from 0.04 to 0.09, with a median of 0.06. Coefficients were larger for physicians than for nurses and larger when observation sessions were short. Baseline ward compliance explained a substantial share of between-ward variation, so adjusting for it reduced the required number of wards. We provide the coefficients and their confidence intervals for use in planning future trials.

records.title: Contamination between wards in cluster trials of hand hygiene interventions: staff movement and shared equipment
records.abstract: In a completed trial of ward-level hand hygiene feedback, 22 percent of nursing shifts on control wards were worked by staff who also worked on intervention wards during the trial. Compliance among these float staff on control wards rose during the trial, and the difference between arms was about a third smaller than among staff who worked on one ward only. Shared portable equipment and joint handovers also carried feedback messages between wards. The authors recommend randomising pairs of wards that share staff as one cluster and recording float status for every observed opportunity.

records.title: Alcohol-based hand rub consumption as a proxy for hand hygiene compliance: agreement with direct observation on 30 wards
records.abstract: We compared monthly alcohol-based hand rub consumption per 1,000 patient-days with directly observed compliance on 30 wards over one year. The correlation between consumption and observed compliance was weak (r equal to 0.31), and consumption rose with patient acuity and with the number of visitors independently of observed staff behaviour. Consumption was cheap to collect and complete for every ward-month, but pump dispensers refilled from bulk stock were recorded inconsistently on six wards. The authors suggest consumption as a context measure rather than as a substitute for observed compliance.

response.synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. One ward-randomised trial reported a large rise in electronic compliance with real-time feedback (48 to 71 against 50 to 54 percent), measured by the feedback system itself, with a smaller difference in observed compliance. A review of 31 studies and a staff study show why the system's own figure is a weak outcome: detection is incomplete and staff can satisfy the badge without cleaning their hands. Visible observers roughly triple hand hygiene events. Planning values for clustering are available (median intracluster correlation 0.06), float staff carry feedback between wards, and infections are too rare to compare in one hospital. Hand rub consumption is a weak proxy.
response.gradeRationale: One randomised trial with a system-measured primary outcome and several observational and methods records; direction consistent for electronic compliance but serious risk of measurement bias and indirectness for real hand hygiene. Certainty that feedback improves actual hand hygiene is low.
response.summary: Eight retrieved records appraised; six source-derived claims recorded with passages; overall certainty low.

response.reading: Real-time feedback acts on the badge figure directly and on hand hygiene only through staff behaviour, so the system's own compliance figure can rise without cleaner hands. Visible observation changes behaviour, float staff carry feedback between wards, and infections are too rare to be the outcome. The design problem is therefore measurement and contamination, not the intervention.

response.rationale: The board's question is whether switching on feedback causes better hand hygiene, and the 16 wards can be randomised because the intervention is a software switch. A cluster randomised trial with pairs of wards that share float staff randomised together limits contamination (c5); the primary outcome is direct observation by external observers, equally visible on both arms, because the system's own figure can be gamed (c3) and visible observation inflates compliance (c2). The retrieved trial (c1) suggests an effect large enough to be worth testing. Reporting follows the CONSORT extension for cluster trials.

steps.value: Correction notice from the authors: an error in the dispenser-to-zone mapping on the feedback wards counted dispenser activations in corridors as hand hygiene at patient-zone entry. After re-analysis with corrected mapping, electronic compliance rose from 48 to 55 percent on feedback wards and from 50 to 54 percent on control wards (difference in change 3 percentage points, 95 percent CI -4 to 10). Directly observed compliance, measured on a random sample of shifts by observers who knew ward allocation, was 64 against 57 percent. The conclusion that real-time feedback increased compliance is withdrawn; the authors now report no clear difference in electronic compliance.

response.overview: Two-arm cluster randomised trial on 16 adult wards randomised in eight pairs of wards that share float staff: four pairs switch on real-time badge feedback with weekly dashboards and four continue silent monitoring, from January to June 2027. The planning basis is under review because the retrieved trial's record has changed.
response.population: Hand hygiene opportunities at patient-zone entry by all staff groups on the 16 wards; float and agency staff included and flagged.
response.exposure: Real-time vibration feedback within ten seconds of patient-zone entry without hand hygiene, and weekly ward dashboards shown at the safety huddle.
response.procedures: Pairs are allocated by computer-generated sequence stratified by medical or surgical specialty. External observers from the regional network observe 25 hours per ward in sessions at random times, wearing the same visible identification on both arms; they record opportunity type, staff group, float status and hand hygiene. Badge data are extracted at ward level for the secondary outcome.

response.designSummary: Cluster randomised trial, 16 wards in 8 pairs, analysed at the opportunity level with ward as the cluster.
response.sampleSize: With 8 wards per arm, about 300 observed opportunities per ward, an intracluster correlation of 0.06 (median of the retrieved estimates, range 0.04 to 0.09) and compliance near 60 percent, the design effect is about 19. Using a t distribution with 14 degrees of freedom, the trial has 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 to detect a difference of about 18 percentage points, or about 15 points after adjustment for ward baseline compliance. The corrected report of the retrieved trial now gives a 3-point difference on the system's measure, far below what 16 wards can detect, so the planning basis must be re-reviewed before the decision is acted on.
response.primaryAnalysis: Mixed-effects logistic regression of observed hand hygiene on arm with a random intercept for ward, adjusted for ward baseline compliance and specialty, with small-sample degrees-of-freedom correction; the difference is reported as a risk difference with its confidence interval.
response.secondaryAnalysis: The same model for badge-system compliance; the difference between badge and observed compliance by arm; hand rub consumption per 1,000 patient-days; float and non-float staff reported separately.
response.missingData: Unobserved sessions are rescheduled within the same month; wards that lose more than 20 percent of sessions are reported, and no opportunity is imputed.
response.multiplicity: One primary comparison; secondary outcomes reported with confidence intervals and no significance claims.
response.software: R with lme4; allocation sequence and analysis code held by the trial statistician.
overfittingGuards: Two adjustment variables fixed in advance
No subgroup testing beyond the float staff split
Allocation concealed from ward managers until switch-on
response.summary: About 15 points detectable with baseline adjustment; the corrected planning value is far smaller, so the design needs re-review.

response.risks: Minimal for patients; for staff, the risk is that feedback feels like surveillance and that ward data are misused. Night alerts may disturb patients in shared bays.
response.consent: Wards are the unit of randomisation and staff are the participants whose behaviour is observed. Individual consent for observation is impracticable without distorting behaviour; the ethics board will be asked for a waiver of individual consent under the Ottawa Statement for cluster trials, with staff informed through the staff council, posters and huddles and able to raise concerns.
response.data: Observers record staff group and float status, never names; badge data are used at ward level only under agreement JSC-2026-07; data are kept on the infection prevention team's restricted drive.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: float, agency and junior staff have least control over workload and may experience feedback as surveillance most. Acceptability and compliance are reported by staff group, and no individual or staff-group data are shared with managers.
response.effectiveness: The trial decides whether a hospital-wide licence is worth buying; a precise null result on the observed outcome is as useful to the board as a positive one.
response.efficiency: Uses installed badges and 400 donated observer-hours.
response.costs: Feedback licence for eight wards for six months, provided by the vendor at no charge for the trial, and observer travel.
response.grants: None needed; an infection prevention research award could fund video-based outcome assessment in a follow-on trial.
response.partnerships: Staff council and unions, the regional infection prevention network (observers), ward managers, and two patient representatives from the infection prevention patient panel.
response.rebPath: Full review by the hospital research ethics board as a cluster randomised trial with a waiver of individual staff consent, following ICH-GCP and the Ottawa Statement; registration in a public trial registry before randomisation.
response.limitations: Observer visibility remains; six months may be too short for durable change; infections are not an evaluable outcome.
response.summary: Cluster trial with a staff consent waiver request, ward-level data use only, and equity reporting by staff group.

response.partnershipPlan: Staff council representatives review the information sheet and data rules; two patient representatives review the alert policy for shared bays; ward managers join the steering group without access to individual data.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; comments on the staff intranet thread about the badge system are summarised without names.

response.title: Real-time electronic feedback and directly observed hand hygiene compliance on hospital wards: a paired cluster randomised trial
response.abstract: Objective: to test whether real-time badge feedback with weekly ward dashboards increases directly observed hand hygiene compliance compared with silent monitoring. Design: cluster randomised trial of 16 adult wards randomised in eight pairs sharing float staff, January to June 2027. Primary outcome: compliance at patient-zone entry observed by external observers equally visible on both arms. Results and conclusions will be written after the trial.
response.introduction: Electronic monitoring vendors report large gains in compliance, but most evaluations measure the outcome with the feedback system itself. The only retrieved randomised trial has since corrected its main result.
response.methods: Pairs of wards sharing float staff are allocated by a stratified sequence. External observers record opportunities in random sessions. The primary analysis is a mixed-effects logistic model adjusted for ward baseline compliance and specialty.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present the flow of wards and observation sessions, observed and badge compliance by arm, and results for float staff separately.
response.discussion: The discussion will compare observed and badge-measured effects, consider observer visibility and contamination, and state what the result means for the licence.
response.limitations: Observer visibility; 16 wards; infections not evaluable; the planning effect size rests on a corrected record.
response.conclusion: To be written after the trial; it will be limited to observed compliance and will not claim effects on infection.
response.reportingChecklist: CONSORT extension for cluster randomised trials
response.summary: CONSORT-structured draft with results left empty until the trial ends.
